📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

von Next Generation am 23.09.2026 in den Kategorien Premier League,Uncategorized mit 0 Kommentaren.

Industry observers note that brBrighton arrived at the match fresh off a 3–2 win at Old Trafford, while Arsenal boasted a clean defensive record and a reputation for controlling games and seeing them out like few other teams in Europe. The match ended 3–0, sparking immense hype around Brighton’s pressing. This analysis explores the underlying mechanisms: their man-oriented pressing across the entire pitch, their asymmetrical build-up play, their transition behavior after winning the ball, and the three goals themselves.

According to recent reports, arteta’s Arsenal are among the best sides in Europe at controlling games out of possession. Any opponent who sets out to establish order is playing on the ground Arsenal own. Hürzeler therefore decided against control – not control surrendered in the sense of a low block, but a chaotic game state that Brighton generated themselves and were therefore prepared for.

System & movement with the ball – FC Arsenal.

System & movement with the ball – Brighton & Hove Albion.

According to recent reports, the thread running through ninety minutes: Arsenal were not to settle into an organised phase either with or without the ball. Three decisions delivered that. The build-up was set up asymmetrically – on the right Brighton prepared the long ball and occupied the landing zone before it was played, on the left counter-movements opened the short route. It was never long instead of short, but two prepared options that would have demanded opposite answers from Arsenal. After regains the ball was not secured but risked immediately, because a secured ball gives the opponent exactly the seconds they need to reorganise. And the press lived off intensity and constantly newly introduced starting points: when a line was played through, Brighton did not stand still but re-established their shape and triggered again.

All three decisions give up ball control in the classical sense. Control came instead from preparation – if you know where the ball will land and you are standing there beforehand, you control the situation without the ball.

According to recent reports, what followed can be pinned to a single number: 41 Arsenal turnovers in their own danger zone. That is not a figure a side of this quality produces because they play badly, but because they never reached the game state their build-up is designed for.

Brightons manorientated press against a 4-3-3.

Sources indicate that the press was simple in principle and demanding in execution. Brighton set up with man-reference to their direct opponent and switched into pure man-marking on the trigger. Against a side that tracks from the first second, marking assignments can be pulled apart by movement before any pressure exists; Brighton refused to offer that, because their shape stayed compact until the trigger moment.

In the “mid-block,” positioned +1 on the last line, but ready at any moment to transition into a high press upon a pressing trigger.

The steering began with Ayari. He curved his pressing run so that Konsa stayed in his cover shadow and Raya was forced to the other side. Kostoulas marked Gabriel, while Chema Andrés and Groß pushed aggressively onto Arsenal’s No. 8s. Groß in particular tracked the dropping Rice and at times advanced into the first pressing line, in some sequences all the way onto Konsa. That requires Rice to be picked up by a team-mate in the same moment – the man-marking worked through handovers as much as through tracking. Centrally, the striker and the No. 10 rotated accordingly: whoever had the shorter route to the next man on the ball pushed out, while the other covered behind him and took over again on the next trigger.

Recent findings suggest that it only held up because the centre-backs came with it. Vušković and Struijk stepped out onto Ødegaard and the dropping Havertz and prevented an underload in central areas. When Arsenal built with three in the first line, Brighton kept one centre-back zonal in the back line – but with permanent reference to the unmarked player in the No. 6 space, stepping onto him the moment the press was triggered. Arsenal’s numerical advantage in build-up therefore never translated into a free man anywhere on the pitch.

Raya was part of the marking scheme too. Ayari’s cover shadow left only the route through a No. 6, and under man-marking that is not an escape but a duel that begins with the first touch. Raya’s body shape reinforced it: he tended to open only half-way, which effectively removed the switch to the far side from his repertoire. Steered onto his right foot, only the right-hand build-up side remained; the left lay open for long stretches and was unreachable for the one player who could have found it.

Every back pass served as a trigger. When the ball went back to Raya or the centre-backs, Brighton pushed up as a unit and raised the defensive line. The density around the ball came less from the base shape than from the recovery runs: players who had been beaten sprinted back, and they did not run at the ball but with a cover shadow onto the lay-off option behind it. An Arsenal player with a marker in his back therefore had neither the lay-off nor the chance to turn.

Recent findings suggest that this is precisely where Brighton differed from most sides who get played through against Arsenal. The usual response is to stay deep once a line has been broken and wait for the shape to settle. Brighton instead pushed up into the next line and used the mid-block to prepare the next jump back into the high press – even when that press had just been beaten. The press therefore had not one starting point per possession, but a steady supply of new ones, and Arsenal had to solve the same pressure several times within a single attack.

Arsenal’s core problem was the absence of a threat in behind. Their attempts to play through the press came without pace beyond the back line, so Brighton were never forced to turn towards their own goal. That made the press cheap: no threat in behind, therefore no need to drop the line. There are three answers to committed man-marking – movement that drags your own marker away and opens space for a third player, a dribble that beats the assignment one-on-one, or a target man who wins the long balls. Arsenal produced none of them.

According to recent reports, when the high press was beaten, Brighton dropped into a 5-1-4 and inverted the priority. The five in the last line formed a deliberate overload against Arsenal’s front line – in exactly the moment a man-oriented side is most vulnerable, because its players are facing forward while the opponents are already moving. Brighton took the depth out of the situation first and only then thought about the ball again.

In a recent development, A “mid-block” in a 5-1-4 formation. The foremost players protected the “red zone” by using their cover shadows and shifting extremely compactly. Arsenal was mostly forced to play around the block, repeatedly giving Brighton time to reorganize.

It has been revealed that A single No. 6 held the connection in front, while the four most advanced players stayed narrow and closed the centre with cover shadows rather than pressing the ball carrier. Arsenal found no central switch on the ball-near side and had to play around the block. Every trip around it cost seconds that Brighton used to shift across, so the end of the route offered the same congestion as the start. In some phases six players stood in the last line.

The block was not a terminus. At every Arsenal back pass Brighton jumped out again and restarted the high press – the same trigger as in the high phase, only from a deeper starting position. The spare man in the last line made that possible, usually Vušković: because the overload left him without a fixed opponent, he could step out, cover the depth and pick up a man himself a moment later. That freed a midfielder to push forward without leaving an assignment open behind him – precisely the point at which sides with a similar approach usually come apart.

In the “mid-block” phase, the “+1” players organized themselves to execute early handovers and jump into pressing situations. Here, Vuskovic—acting as the “+1” player from the defensive line—steps up to pick up the Arsenal player operating in the number 10 position.

Sources indicate that on top of that came the trap on the touchline. Once Brighton steered the ball wide, players jumped in from every direction: the ball-near winger closed the route back, the No. 6 covered inside, the back line stepped out. The back pass, the switch and the ball in behind did not disappear one after another but at the same time. Take away only the back pass and a side switches play; take away only the switch and they play backwards and start again. When all that remains is an individual action against several opponents with the touchline at your back, it almost always ends with the opposition.

In a recent development, after a regain there are two basic options: risk the ball immediately to launch the attack, or secure it to establish order. Hürzeler consistently chose the first, and it follows directly from the overall idea – a secured ball would have given Arsenal exactly the seconds in which their structure reorganises.

When a high press was bypassed, Brighton succeeded in forcing Arsenal into congested situations in the area in front of the back four. In doing so, the players who had been bypassed shifted to block the passing lanes of the players positioned behind the ball. This created additional pressure on the ball carrier, who was simultaneously facing pressure from the front via a “negative” pressing movement (i.e., pressing towards their own goal).

It has been revealed that the counter was prepared before the regain. When Arsenal found a player in the No. 6 space after beating the press, Brighton immediately closed his back pass, so the turnover inevitably occurred in a moment when Arsenal were all ahead of the ball. The density around the ball, a defensive necessity, meant in attack that Brighton were central and therefore on the shortest route to goal. The first ball went to the deepest player, followed by a dribble at speed into the box, with no intermediate step and no square pass for safety.

Recent findings suggest that in the build-up phase, Brighton utilized a diamond shape. De Cuyper and Boscagli engaged in a 2v2 duel on the left flank, while Kostoulas, Gomez, and Kadioglu created a high 3v3 situation on the right. Briefly, both center-backs and a defensive midfielder would spread out to widen the formation. Additional support occasionally came from Groß, dropping back from the number 10 position. Ayari occupied Konsa and Gabriel through constant runs into the open spaces ahead of him.

In a recent development, in deep build-up Brighton baited Arsenal in deliberately. Verbruggen put his foot on the ball while the centre-backs split and lengthened the pressing runs of their opponents. On paper that produced a 3v2 against Arsenal’s first line – except Hürzeler had no intention of playing through that overload on the ground. 25 of 40 goalkeeper passes were long, 62.5 per cent, and they went overwhelmingly to the right.

Industry observers note that the structure allowed for a long ball to the right flank, feeding into the 3-3 formation. This created opportunities to contest the second ball or flick on the aerial pass. Additionally, Vuskovic offered a short, low passing option as the free player.

There, Brighton consistently created a 3v3 – an intact structure for the second ball regardless of whether the first contact was won. That is exactly what separates it from an ordinary long ball: the action was not judged by the aerial duel but by the situation that followed it. Kostoulas dropping added to the disorganisation of Arsenal’s high line, because a centre-back had to decide whether to follow him between the lines or let him turn. After winning second balls Brighton played on at high speed and looked for an early shot or an early cross, even against a defensive overload – again the decision for tempo over the clean attack.

Once again, the 3-3 structure on the right flank. Here, from open play.

On the left Brighton worked through pinning rather than through length. Boscagli stepping inside dragged Saka into central areas and took him out of the wide zone Arsenal needed him in defensively, while De Cuyper dropped and offered the mid-range diagonal once the assignments had been pulled apart. The asymmetry was a personnel decision: the players for second balls were on the right, the players who could drag markers out of position on the left. Arsenal would have had to condense against one side and hand over assignments cleanly against the other.

Recent findings suggest that the team’s build-up play was asymmetrical, featuring a high, wide approach on the right contrasted with the left flank: Boscagli often played an inverted role—supplementing the existing diamond formation—which opened up space for de Cuyper. Meanwhile, Groß and Kostoulas occupied the players on Arsenal’s right defensive flank, enabling Brighton to find low-ball solutions against the press.

Industry observers note that with the ball in midfield there were two patterns. The first was the deliberate back pass to Verbruggen to pull Arsenal’s block out, followed by the same long-short structure as in deep build-up. The back pass was not a safety option here but the tool that created the space behind the pressing line in the first place.

The second pattern worked through central and wide tension at high speed, supplemented by rotations within their own structure. Arsenal repeatedly failed to hand over their pressing assignments in a coordinated way against it – the same weakness Brighton had solved cleanly in their own press. In possession Brighton’s shape approached a 4-3-3: Chema Andrés as the deepest No. 6, Groß with freedom from the left half-space, Kadıoğlu pushing up early to support Gómez, Boscagli starting slightly deeper on the left.

The 1-0 by Groß in the 31st minute is the whole initiative in one sequence. Brighton play back to the goalkeeper from midfield, go long, lose the first contact and win the second ball. After a phase of circulation the next attack meets a back line that has already been destabilised: Kostoulas drops, Arsenal’s midfield and Konsa step out, and Kostoulas lays the ball back against the direction of the pressure to Groß. Because Ayari runs in behind at the same time, Arsenal’s defenders drop – and Groß has the time for the shot from around 20 metres. In the build-up Brighton had used rotations to drag Guimarães over to the left.

Sources indicate that the opening goal stems from a positional attack. Kostoulas spots open space and makes a run into it. With a pass played across his standing leg, he feeds the ball to Groß in the space between the lines. As Groß takes a few quick touches and dribbles toward the defensive line, Gabriel and Calafiori drop back together, thereby opening up a shooting lane.

It has been revealed that the 2-0 by Kostoulas shortly before half-time follows the same logic from the opposite direction. After a set piece of their own, Brighton clear an Arsenal counter and transition again immediately, 4v5 in Arsenal’s half, and once more the shot comes from distance while the centre-backs drop off.

Much like the goal that made it 1–0, both defenders went to ground near the ball carrier, thereby opening up space for the goalscorer—this time arising from a transition situation.

It has been revealed that both goals share the same cause: Arsenal’s centre-backs stepped out too late to press the man between the lines. React only when the shooting motion starts and you cannot get into the block from 20 to 25 metres. What is striking is that this passivity is the same one Arsenal showed in their own build-up – a side that does not leave its position to offer itself does not leave it to close down a shooter either.

The 3-0 by Chema Andrés came from a corner: Groß delivered from the left, Brighton had created an overload at the far post and protected it with two blocks, and Chema rose completely unmarked to head in off the inside of the post.

According to recent reports, two goals up, many sides would have defended deeper. Brighton came out with unchanged and at times higher pressing intensity, and the coordination was visibly drilled: marking assignments were swapped cleanly even in dynamic situations, and Arsenal’s structural adjustments were absorbed.

Arsenal had managed a few organised possession phases in Brighton’s half in the first period; in the second it became harder. In those phases they built with a back three, Rice as the third centre-back, Ødegaard dropping alongside Guimarães and the full-backs occupying the half-spaces. Arteta reacted around the hour: Zubimendi and Merino for Timber and Guimarães, with Rice moving to right-back, followed shortly by Gyökeres and Eze for Ødegaard and Tzolis. There was no noticeable effect, because the problem did not lie in the shape but in the assignments in front of it.

There was also a layer that usually goes missing in analysis: Brighton used tactical fouls deliberately to stop Arsenal finding a rhythm. Arteta admitted afterwards that the game had been “very difficult to control”, pointing to lost first and second balls and to Brighton’s directness.

In a recent development, arteta’s Arsenal being outplayed this clearly is rare. That it happened proactively and aggressively is rarer still – most sides who take something from Arsenal do it with a low block and efficiency. Hürzeler deliberately stepped back afterwards and praised his players’ courage, which gets to the heart of it: the plan only works if eleven players are willing to carry it through in every single sequence.

It has been revealed that the interesting question is where the idea came from. Chelsea were a common opponent: Brighton had 74 per cent possession there and lost 3-4 against a counter-attacking side – control right down to the numbers, without return. Alonso’s Chelsea tried the opposite route against Arsenal, a deliberate surrender of control, also without success. The likely derivation lies between the two: neither give up control nor chase it, but generate the unsettled game state yourself and be prepared for it.

There is no reason for panic at Arsenal, but Arteta will need answers against a high press. The build-up was predictable for long stretches, and above all the direct option with pace in behind was missing as a threat. As long as that does not exist, a man-oriented press costs very little against this side.

For Brighton the open question is repeatability. Man-marking of this commitment, collective recovery runs with cover shadows and a touchline trap that requires everyone to trigger at once are hard to produce twice in an English week. Whether the proposal works was answered on this afternoon. How often it can be produced will decide the season.

LC can often be found in the classroom, preferably on the soccer field, and—on rare occasions—on LinkedIn.

#50098. The Harriers of Norway: welcome to the most unlikely Kidderminster supporters club

📅 30 Jan 2023 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1464 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Thesefootballtimes ↗ Open Full Page

The Harriers of Norway: welcome to the most unlikely Kidderminster supporters club

📅 30 Jan 2023 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1464 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Thesefootballtimes

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that on the west coast of Norway, spread across the islands of Hessa, Aspøya, Nørvøya and Uksenøya, at the mouth of the Geirangerfjord, lies Ålesund.
  • From its colourful townhouses and their turrets and towers, to its harbourside promenades where the streets shake hands with the sea, Ålesund attracts thousands of visitors a year.
  • According to recent reports, at the junction where Kaiser Wilhems Gate meets Harald Torviks Plass, you can find the Brooklyn Bar.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that on the west coast of Norway, spread across the islands of Hessa, Aspøya, Nørvøya and Uksenøya, at the mouth of the Geirangerfjord, lies Ålesund. It is not a large town, or by in the native Norwegian, but it is a place brimming with appeal. Once razed to the ground at the turn of the 20th century by a devastating fire, it was rebuilt not in wood but stone by the finest Norwegian and German architects of the era.

From its colourful townhouses and their turrets and towers, to its harbourside promenades where the streets shake hands with the sea, Ålesund attracts thousands of visitors a year. Amidst its myriad of paved boulevards, one road in particular is home to a special peculiarity.

According to recent reports, at the junction where Kaiser Wilhems Gate meets Harald Torviks Plass, you can find the Brooklyn Bar. With its glass front glimmering, there appears nothing untoward about this New York-themed establishment, but head inside and you can find, tucked away in a not-so-quiet corner festooned in red and white, Norway’s only supporter group dedicated to English National League North side, Kidderminster Harriers.

Recent findings suggest that in order to find out how a town nearly 800 miles from Worcestershire became home to The Harriers of Norway, These Football Times spoke to the group’s founder, Lars Andreas Vegsund. “It started off as a funny thing when our old boys team needed a English club that didn’t have a supporter club in Scandinavia because we wanted to attend the yearly supporter cup in 2019.”.

Given the popularity of English football in Norway, the Supporters Cup is an key fixture in the calendar. Organised by Supporterunionen for Britisk Fotball (the Supporters Union of British Football), the knockout tournament takes place every year in Oslo and is contested by the various supporter groups of British football teams. Thousands of players and dozens of fan groups are involved, with the 2022 edition seeing Ipswich take the title for the third occasion.

In a recent development, lars explains, “We just started going down the different leagues on our phones and looked for a team that would stand out. When my mate called out ‘Kidderminster’, I shouted ‘Harriers’ and that was it. I’d played with the Harriers on different football management games through the years and it just seemed right.”.

It has been revealed that this Saturday night decision between two mates began as a lonely affair but gathered momentum quickly. By the following week, the pair had found five other Norwegians interested in beginning the Harriers of Norway supporters club and subsequently held their first board meeting in the familiar surrounds of the Brooklyn Bar.

According to recent reports, three years later and the Harriers of Norway can boast 191 members throughout the country in locations as diverse as Bergen, Trondheim, Halden, Mo i Rana and, of course, the capital Oslo. And the common thread unites them all: their affection for an English football club that was last in the Football League in 2005.

But, as Lars is keen to impress, supporting the Harriers is part of a larger agenda. “It has become this rebellion against global football. We enjoy getting back to the roots of English football and getting in touch with proper English football fans, which has been an absolutely mind-blowing experience for us so far. It has surpassed all our expectations.”.

Recent findings suggest that as the Harriers of Norway grew in size, so too did they grow in ambition. With Kidderminster struggling to escape the clutches of the National League North, opportunities for their Norwegian fans to watch live matches are scarce. Therefore, they rely primarily on BBC Hereford and Worcestershire radio commentary to catch the 3pm kick-off before later projecting the YouTube highlights onto the basement wall of an old factory within which they have constructed a replica of the terraces of Aggborough Stadium.

Industry observers note that lars proudly shows off photographs of what they have dubbed the “Ålesund Aggborough” and even supplies us with a video. In it, the camera takes you on a tour down a short corridor festooned with Harriers memorabilia before opening out into an area that is a near-identical imitation of the North Stand (save for the welcome addition of well-stocked bar positioned in one corner, of course). Members lean against the red railings, pints in hand, bedecked in replica shirts of years gone by, as they watch an enormous projection of the latest match on the whitewashed wall.

It is more than a worthy substitute, but it doesn’t quite hold the same allure as the real experience – one which many of the club’s members have sampled for themselves over the preceding years. “We have been [to England] four times so far, but it would of course have been more if there hadn’t been any COVID,” says Lars. “We are looking to get back two more times this season [2022/2023]. We really want to get an away game, and were really gutted when the Scarborough match was called off, but hopefully soon we can get on that away game coach.”.

As for the club itself, they have been extraordinarily accommodating of their Norwegian fans, even going so far as to arrange a Q&A session with their manager Russell Penn, which he hosted from his own kitchen, no less. Then, during a September 2022 tour, the Norwegian supporters were invited to watch first-team training where club captain Shane Byrne presented them with a kit signed by the entire squad.

And the kindness didn’t stop with the club itself; local supporters took the Norwegians to a cricket match after the postponement of Kidderminster’s weekend fixture following the death of Queen Elizabeth II.

Because of their steadfast devotion to Kiddy, the Harriers of Norway have been the subject of a TV special by Norwegian broadcaster Viaplay, who travelled to Norway’s west coast to witness the Ålesund Aggborough and interview several supporters, with their segment airing ahead of the third round FA cup tie against West Ham – the Harriers’ most high-profile match since their cup run of 2013/14 which culminated in a 1-0 fourth-round loss to Sunderland at the Stadium of Light.

In a recent development, but when it comes to a hypothetical fixture between Kiddy and his local Norwegian club, Lars is in no doubt as to where his loyalties lie. “Without a doubt, the Harriers. No question. This club and their fans have shown us the true meaning of support and brought us back to our childhood feelings of supporting our ‘own’ team. It has truly been an absolutely amazing experience so far, and I can`t wait to see how far this will take us all.”.

Perhaps one day, they will get to witness their beloved English club in the Football League once more, evoking memories of yesteryear when the deep pockets of retail magnate Lionel Newton finally lifted Kidderminster out of non-league for the first time in their history.

Recent findings suggest that the Harriers had won the Conference before in 1993/94 but had been denied entry to Division Three because of stringent fire safety laws implemented in the wake of the fire at Valley Parade that had claimed 56 lives. At the time, Aggborough’s main stand was constructed mostly out of timber, and despite the construction of a upcoming cantilever stand in time for the new season, the Football League rejected the club’s application.

In a recent development, kidderminster eventually achieved promotion, winning the Conference by nine points in 1999/2000, whereupon they embarked on a four-year stay in the Football League. These were the halcyon days of the Danes, when Jan Mølby held court in Aggborough, ably assisted by star striker “Bomber” Bo Henriksen along with winger Thomas Skovbjerg.

It is a fact not lost on the Scandinavian admirers of today. “I think there has been three playing Danes,” Lars says. “But to have a Norwegian play for Harriers would be a dream come true for us. We can definitely be Harriers’ eyes and ears here in Norway if the right talent reveals up!”.

As of writing, Kidderminster have no Scandinavians, let alone Norwegians, on their books, and are firmly ensconced in the middle order of the National League North, with promotion or relegation seemingly as unlikely as the other. Despite this, that won’t stop the Harriers of Norway from filling the stands of the Ålesund Aggborough each weekend or taking the short flight across the North Sea to the West Midlands when the opportunity arises.

And who knows, maybe one day Kidderminster Harriers won’t just find success on the pitches of the National League but on the artificial turf in Oslo’s Supporters Cup, too.

By Josh Butler @joshisbutler90 Photo: Express & Star.

Industry News: On a déconné avec Da Cunha (22)

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Resté un grand supporter des Verts qui l'ont pourtant recalé plusieurs fois à l'adolescence au grand dam de Dominique Rocheteau, Lucas Da Cunha est "le grand gagnant de l'ère Zidane" comme l'a indiqué aujourd'hui Le Dauphiné Libéré.
  • In a recent development, L'AFP souligne les performances du natif de Roanne (Loire) en équipe de France, jugées "très satisfaisantes" par son sélectionneur.
  • Dans sa dernière édition, la Pravda n'est pas en reste.

Resté un grand supporter des Verts qui l'ont pourtant recalé plusieurs fois à l'adolescence au grand dam de Dominique Rocheteau, Lucas Da Cunha est "le grand gagnant de l'ère Zidane" comme l'a indiqué aujourd'hui Le Dauphiné Libéré.

In a recent development, L'AFP souligne les performances du natif de Roanne (Loire) en équipe de France, jugées "très satisfaisantes" par son sélectionneur. "L'ailier de formation a été placé en meneur de jeu par Cesc Fabregas en Serie A où il s'est révélé après quelques échecs en Ligue 1. Le patron des Bleus l'a encore fait reculer d'un cran en le plaçant dans un rôle de sentinelle où Da Cunha, qui découvrait le poste, a montré beaucoup de promesses et quelques lacunes, en défense notamment. Mais Zidane qui a procédé à une large revue d'effectif lors des deux rassemblements de l'automne, lui a accordé une confiance telle que le capitaine de Côme est le joueur de champ qui compte le plus de temps de jeu à égalité avec Michael Olise (386 minutes chacun).".

Dans sa dernière édition, la Pravda n'est pas en reste. "On dit d'un entraîneur qu'il couche toujours un nom en premier quand il compose son onze de départ. Concernant Zinédine Zidane chez les Bleus, on va finir par penser que ce nom est celui de Lucas Da Cunha, qui avait été le meilleur Français lors de la défaite en ltalie. Contre la Turquie, le meneur de jeu reculé a cherché à accélérer la circulation de balle des Bleus, qui manquait souvent de verticalité, tout en grattant plusieurs ballons au pressing ou grâce à ses anticipations (7 récupérations, record du match côté français). Depuis sa position basse, il est capable de renverser le jeu pour donner de l'air à l'équipe, mais aussi d'offrir de très bons ballons de but, comme il l'a fait deux fois pour Kylian Mbappé en dépassant son poste de sentinelle.".

"Déjà un pilier de l'ère Zidane" dixit Le Parisien, le joueur de 25 ans savoure sur TF1. "Les compliments de Zidane sont géniaux, c’est exceptionnel. Il m’a donné beaucoup de responsabilités depuis que je suis arrivé. J’essaie d’appliquer tout ce qu’il me demande, que ce soit sur le plan défensif ou offensif. Je sens que j'ai encore une grosse marge de progression, c'est ça qui est super intéressant pour moi. C’est sûr que l’ascension est folle. Il y a encore quelques années, j’étais ailier. Aujourd’hui, je suis milieu de terrain et je suis là avec les Bleus. Quand on commence le foot, quand on est jeune, c’est un rêve de pouvoir porter ce maillot. On rêve de ça. Et le jour où ça arrive, on n’y croit pas trop. J’adore, j’y prends goût. C’est une grande fierté d’être ici.".

#50093. Bobby Robson, Ipswich Town and a brutal quest for the 1981 treble

📅 31 Jan 2023 • ⏱️ 21m • 📚 Deep Dive (4222 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Thesefootballtimes ↗ Open Full Page

Bobby Robson, Ipswich Town and a brutal quest for the 1981 treble

📅 31 Jan 2023 | ⏱️ 21 min read (4222 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Thesefootballtimes

⏱️ ~21 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The wind blows hard and cold across East Anglia during the winter.
  • Recent findings suggest that while both teams are small in comparison to those from the major cities of England – London, Liverpool and Manchester for example – they’ve famously punched above their weight in times gone by.
  • But overall, Ipswich have enjoyed more success, beginning with the appointment of Alf Ramsey as manager back in August 1955, when they were languishing in the Third Division (South) – a provincial team with no success to their name.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The wind blows hard and cold across East Anglia during the winter. With barely a hill in sight, there is nothing to stop the progress of the icy chill in this south east corner of England. An agricultural region, it is home to two principal football teams – Norwich City in Norfolk and Ipswich Town in Suffolk.

Recent findings suggest that while both teams are small in comparison to those from the major cities of England – London, Liverpool and Manchester for example – they’ve famously punched above their weight in times gone by. Norwich were particularly strong just after the Premier League began, finishing third in in the inaugural season before a famous UEFA Cup victory over the mighty Bayern Munich.

But overall, Ipswich have enjoyed more success, beginning with the appointment of Alf Ramsey as manager back in August 1955, when they were languishing in the Third Division (South) – a provincial team with no success to their name.

It has been revealed that having played for England 32 times, including the infamous 1950 World Cup defeat to the US, Ramsey hung up his boots in 1955 and set about considering the next phase of his career. A player with a reputation for the tactical side of the game, it seemed natural that he would gravitate towards coaching. And so he was approached by the owners of Ipswich, the Cobbold Brewing family, to consider a player-manager role after their latest relegation to the third tier of English football.

Dismissing the playing role, he agreed to join them as manager at the age of 35. Everyone has to start somewhere, so while Ipswich were a small club languishing in the lower leagues, Ramsey was hoping it might be a stepping-stone to bigger things.

No-one around Ipswich could possibly have dreamed about what would happen next. In his second season he secured promotion to the Second Division as champions with a team scoring over 100 goals, which was subsequently followed by a Second Division championship and promotion to the big-time.

Sources indicate that incredibly, Ramsey then led Ipswich to become vhampions of England in their maiden campaign in the top-flight, an incredible achievement over the course of just four seasons. It was this amazing debut in management that led England to come knocking in 1963 – and the rest, as they say, is history.

Unfortunately, Ipswich didn’t build on this success and bumped between the First and Second tiers until the arrival of yet another future England managing great, Bobby Robson, in January 1969. Over the next decade, Robson built Ipswich into a successful side once again, the pinnacle being FA Cup glory in 1978 following a 1-0 victory over Arsenal, which could have been a much wider margin, such was Ipswich’s domination on the day.

Recent findings suggest that they were a regular top-five team over this period and a constant thorn in the side of more established teams such as Liverpool and Manchester United. This was personified in an incredible game during the 1979/80 season when Ipswich demolished Manchester United 6-0 at home despite the United goalkeeper saving two penalties. One question remained, however: could Robson take Ipswich one step further and convert a top five team into English champions against the mighty Liverpool?

It was against this backdrop that 1980/81 commenced. Ipswich had finished a strong third during the previous campaign, but behind both Manchester United and the dominant Liverpool team of the time. This was the Liverpool of Clemence, Neal, Hansen, Thompson, Case, Lee, McDermott, Souness and Dalglish. This was the Liverpool who not only won the title but also reached the semi-finals of both the League Cup and the FA Cup, managed by the legendary Bob Paisley. This was the Liverpool who dominated the late 1970s, having won four of the previous five campaigns. They were not going to give up their position of dominance lightly.

While the Liverpool squad sent shivers through all who met them, Robson had assembled a formidable squad of his own in his little corner of Suffolk. In goal was Paul Cooper, a keeper who joined Ipswich in 1974 and enjoyed a reputation as a penalty specialist. The defence included internationals such as George Burley, Terry Butcher, Mick Mills and Russell Osman. In fact, the England back line around that time often included Butcher, Mills and Osman, so good a defensive unit were they. But it was in midfield that things got especially interesting.

In the 1970s, English football was still extremely insular. It was widely thought that foreign players were unable to cope with the rigors of English physicality and would wilt on a cold, rainy night in January. And really, who wanted all that fancy dribbling and passing that these continentals would bring over? English football was not a game for finesse.

In a recent development, against this backdrop, Robson decided to buck the trend and go shopping overseas. In doing so, he brought in not one but two Dutch gems. The city of Enschede lies close to the German border and is home of FC Twente, and it is from there that Robson signed two midfielders in 1979, Arnold Muhren and Frans Thijssen.

Recent findings suggest that the year before had seen Tottenham enjoy success with the double-signing of Ossie Ardiles and Ricky Villa, but the import of two non-British players was still a novelty at the time. The signing would prove to be a Robson masterstroke, bringing in two players with the ability to play the ball on the ground with an advanced level of skill.

Sources indicate that he then just needed someone else in that midfield to provide a bit more “British grit”. Luckily exactly that player had joined Ipswich in 1975 to mature into one of the top players in England by 1980.

To call John Wark combative is an understatement; he personified teamwork with energy that was second to none. Like Bryan Robson, he was a midfielder with the engine of a Rolls-Royce, who could run all day and shared the speciality of popping up in the area and scoring. For a midfielder, Wark had a phenomenal goalscoring record: he would end his Ipswich career with 94 goals from 266 appearances. And 1980/81 was going to see him in his prime.

Recent findings suggest that in attack, when Wark wasn’t dashing in to score, Eric Gates, Paul Mariner and Alan Brazil supplied plenty of firepower. Gates had played for Ipswich his whole career after making his debut at just 18 in 1973, with his finest moment coming when he netted both goals in a 2-1 win over Barcelona at Portman Road in the 1979 Cup Winners Cup quarter-final.

Sources indicate that mariner, meanwhile, had been a club-record signing from Plymouth for the princely fee of £220,000 and had established himself as an England target man under Ron Greenwood. Alan Brazil also enjoyed status as an international within Scotland.

Industry observers note that so going into the 1980/81 season, while their squad may not have been as deep as Liverpool, it was packed with established internationals from England, Scotland and the Netherlands. Providing the key players could keep injury-free, there was no reason why they couldn’t push on to new heights. They also had a UEFA cup campaign to look forward to.

As they travelled to Leicester on the opening day, there was a cautious mood of optimism amongst the fans. That optimism was soon justified as Ipswich started the season in fine form. After winning the opener at Filbert Street, they proceeded to win seven of their first eight league fixtures. In the days of two points for a win, they opened up a four-point gap on Liverpool, Everton and a developing Aston Villa.

It has been revealed that wark was showing his uncanny goalscoring ability with six goals in those eight games as both Villa and Everton were defeated at Portman Road, the latter 4-0. But October would prove a more realistic test with trips to both Liverpool and Manchester United looming.

September also saw Ipswich begin their UEFA cup campaign, Wark again going on a scoring spree, netting four goals – including a hat-trick of penalties – at Portman Road against Aris Salonika, giving Ipswich a 5-1 victory which would be enough despite a 3-1 defeat back in Cyprus. A pattern would develop over the campaign of winning at home but losing away.

Sources indicate that back in the league, October saw Ipswich travel to Anfield and come away with a respectable draw thanks to a Thijssen goal. They followed that with another 1-1 draw at home to Manchester United. They had played the top two teams from the previous season and maintained their unbeaten record. The end of October did, however, see Aston Villa take the top spot, albeit only two points ahead of Ipswich who had two games in hands over the Villains.

According to recent reports, the end of October saw Ipswich’s next European adventure as, once again, a first leg win at home saw them establish a 3-0 win over Bohemians Prague, with Wark inevitably scoring twice, before another away leg scare that saw them lose 2-0 but hang on to progress to the third round. Wark now had six European goals to go along with his impressive domestic tally and seemed to be single-handedly dragging Ipswich along.

Industry observers note that it was game 15 of the season that finally saw Ipswich suffer their first defeat – and surprisingly it occurred away at basement-dwellers Brighton. But they immediately bounced back with back-to-back wins to finish November in third, behind Villa and Liverpool but still with three games in hand. The end of November also saw Portman Road again host a UEFA Cup first leg – against Widzew Lodz of Poland – on a night few would forget.

Sources indicate that widzew had impressively knocked out Manchester United and Juventus in the preceding two rounds and included a young striker who was getting quite the reputation by the name of Zbigniew Boniek. Juve decided to continue to monitor his progress, leading to his eventual signing and successful partnership with Michel Platini at the Delle Alpi.

Sources indicate that but on this night in November, they would be swept aside 5-0 by Ipswich, inclusive of another Wark hat-trick. Of course, Ipswich then went on to lose the return leg in Poland 1-0, but the Portman Road faithful now truly believed. The European adventure was in full flight but would now be on hold until March. Until then, it was back to blustery cold Suffolk for a continued league campaign and the start of the FA Cup.

December saw six league games including a home draw against Liverpool, a much-enjoyed home victory in the East Anglian derby over Norwich, and just one defeat away at Tottenham. By month’s end, Ipswich were just a single point behind leaders Liverpool and Villa, but still with two games in hand. Attention now turned to the FA Cup.

Sources indicate that the FA Cup still retained its magic back in the 80s with full-strength teams sent out, fan fever and budding romance. Ipswich had enjoyed a strong bond with the competition in recent times, winning it in 1978, and so it was with excitement that fans awaited the draw to see how their latest campaign would commence. The beauty of the open FA Cup draw delivered, throwing Ipswich a third-round tie at home against Aston Villa.

According to recent reports, unsurprisingly it would prove to be a tight game, but a moment of magic from the Dutch duo led to an early Mariner goal, which proved enough on the night. The reward was a fourth-round tie away at Second Division Shrewsbury.

As evident in their UEFA Cup campaign, Ipswich had a poor track record away from home in the cups, and that continued at Gay Meadow as the Tractor Boys came away with a 0-0 draw in a game that Robson admitted they were lucky to have survived. Ipswich’s home form saw them win the replay 3-0 and set up a fifth-round tie in February at home to Charlton.

According to recent reports, ipswich’s January league campaign saw them win three and draw one, scoring 11 goals over the three games, a strong run that saw them return to the top of the table ahead of Aston Villa on goal difference and with champions Liverpool beginning to drop away. It was a stellar month that meant Ipswich were now top of Division One, in the fifth round of the FA Cup and in the quarter-finals of the UEFA Cup.

February saw them build on this momentum as they won all four league games and beat Charlton 2-0 in the FA Cup, leaving them two points ahead of Villa in what was now effectively a head-to-head race and awaiting Nottingham Forest away in an FA Cup quarter-final. The whispers began around England: could Ipswich actually win the treble of league, FA Cup and UEFA Cup? Heady stuff, indeed.

It has been revealed that there was one major obstacle ahead in terms of the treble. March saw Ipswich return to Europe, and the UEFA Cup draw had given them the toughest of ties: St-Etienne. Three-time league champions during the 1970s and European Cup runners-up in 1976, it was a squad that boasted the likes of Battiston, Lopez, Larius, Rep and a certain Platini.

This was the Platini who would soon be joining Boniek in Turin and who would win European Footballer of the Year in 1983, ’84 and ’85. It was a team with serious European pedigree – and Ipswich had to travel to the Stade Geoffery-Guichard first.

It was a legendary night for the boys from Suffolk. Gates were closed two hours ahead of kick-off as 42,000 crammed into the stadium. It was 26 years since St-Etienne had last lost a European tie at home. An early headed goal from Dutch star Rep in the iconic green shirt had the crowd whipped into a frenzy as Ipswich’s poor away cup form continued. But then a powerful header from Mariner left the teams level at the half. And then the miracle occurred.

Just two minutes from the restart, some nice interplay from Ipswich saw Wark pass the ball to Muhren outside the area. Without hesitating, Muhren unleashed a left-foot screamer into the top corner, giving the goalkeeper no chance. Ipswich had their first UEFA Cup lead away from home.

With confidence surging, a ball out to Brazil on the right saw his cross volleyed by Butcher before Mariner swooped in to score Ipswich’s third. St-Etienne were on the ropes and the knockout blow came from who else but Wark with a strong header into the corner. Ipswich had ended their away curse in style. Robson commented: “We have demolished a good side with one of the best victories anyone has achieved in Europe in the past ten years.”.

Recent findings suggest that as if to reinforce the point, Ipswich then comfortably won the return leg 3-1 in front of a packed Portman Road. Needless to say, Wark was on the scoresheet once again. Suddenly all of Europe was aware of the Tractor Boys.

Industry observers note that in between these two historic games, they also travelled to Nottingham to take on Brian Clough’s Forest in the FA Cup quarter-final. A pulsating tie ensued as Forest literally gifted Ipswich a two-goal lead only to see it evaporate as Trevor Francis, Colin Walsh and John Robertson turned the game on its head.

In a recent development, it seemed that finally the volume of games had caught up with Ipswich and the treble dream was crumbling. But then a shot by Thijssen took a cruel deflection and the blues escaped with a lucky draw. The replay was won 1-0 and the treble dream was back on … just. Ipswich were in the semi-finals of both the FA Cup and UEFA Cup.

Recent findings suggest that but all these games were beginning to drain a small squad and cracks finally began to show during March in their league form. After having lost two games all season, March saw them defeated in successive away games at Manchester United and Leeds. It was enough to still see Ipswich top at the end of the month, just a point ahead of Aston Villa. It was a first ominous sign.

And so the season was coming towards the end with Ipswich entering April top of the league and in two major semi-finals. A historic treble was still in play – if Ipswich could just maintain their momentum through the final weeks. But they were facing eight games during April. With a skeleton squad, they were going to need a reserve of energy and a bout of luck to negotiate such a schedule.

The final nervewracking endgame commenced under the ultimate definition of fixture congestion, and the diary evolved as follows:.

Ipswich visit West Brom in the league and suffer their third successive away loss 3-1 – the irony being that West Brom’s victory helps their arch-rivals Aston Villa.

Ipswich face the first leg of their UEFA semi-final against a powerful Koln at Portman Road, boasting the likes of Littbarski, Bonhof and Dieter Muller. A full house sees Ipswich establish a slim 1-0 first-leg victory courtesy of a header from Wark.

Ipswich travel up to Villa Park for their FA Cup semi-final against Manchester City. A crowd of 46,000 watch a nervy game remain goalless before entering extra time with Beattie having an effort cleared off the line. Then a through ball to City’s Bennett sees him tussle with Butcher, with a free-kick somewhat harshly awarded to City around 30 yards from goal.

Industry observers note that what happened next lives in Manchester City folklore; skipper Paul Power curls the free-kick past Cooper into the top corner. It leaves Ipswich with 20 minutes to rescue the treble dream, but it isn’t to be. It has taken three games in eight days to finally break them, but break them it has. The treble is no more.

Sources indicate that ipswich now have the titanic task of picking themselves up from defeat – and a 120-minute match – to revisit Villa Park just three days later for a possible league decider. After three successive away defeats, a loss here would virtually hand Villa the trophy.

According to recent reports, over 47,000 fans pack Villa Park for the title decider. A hopeful long ball sees Villa defender McNaught under no pressure, except that he fails to notice Mariner closing in behind him. Before he knows what is happening, Mariner pokes the ball from him and Brazil slots Ipswich into the lead. Suddenly the confidence is back and an early second-half Villa surge is thwarted twice by Cooper.

According to recent reports, villa once again go into self-destruct mode as a wayward pass from Bremner allows Mariner to play in Gates for a second Ipswich goal. Villa come back with a beauty from Gary Shaw but Ipswich hang on to rekindle their title hopes. In three days, Ipswich players go from despair to ecstasy on the same Villa Park turf.

Industry observers note that another league game as Ipswich host Arsenal at Portman Road. The endless matches are now taking their toll and Robson chooses to rest Thijssen while Kevin Beattie is absent with a broken arm. Unfortunately, Ipswich finally experience their first home loss of the season as Arsenal leave with a damaging 2-0 victory, with the opening goal initially disallowed for offside before a change of mind following a referee-linesman consultation. An injured Gates has to be substituted during the game to add to Ipswich’s injury woes.

Just two days after their first home defeat of the season, Ipswich must travel to Norwich for the East Anglian derby. If any team will delight in derailing Ipswich’s title push, it will be the Canaries. Almost 26,000 rabid Norwich fans pack Carrow Road to urge their team on. Despite being near the bottom of the table, they shock Ipswich by inflicting a 1-0 defeat. It seems now that the title is heading to Villa Park, much to the delight of those in yellow.

Again, a mere two-day rest and then off to Koln to defend their narrow 1-0 first-leg advantage. An insane schedule for any team but possibly the last leg of the treble still alive. But Ipswich again drag themselves off the canvas and win 1-0, courtesy of an unlikely goalscorer in Butcher, to reach the UEFA Cup final.

Back to Portman Road for a must-win home tie against their FA Cup foes Manchester City. Butcher again becomes the hero as he scores the only goal of the game – and Ipswich are still just in the title race. Two games are left in May to decide the league with two UEFA final legs sandwiched in between against AZ Alkmaar.

In a recent development, with Aston Villa now almost over the finishing line, Ipswich travel to Middlesborough in a must-win game while Villa travel to Arsenal. Arsenal win 2-0 but play against a backdrop of singing Villa fans as the news circulates around Highbury that Ipswich are losing at Ayresome Park. The defeat means that the second part of the treble dream is officially over as Villa are crowned Division One champions. In the space of under a month, two legs of the stool have been removed. Only the UEFA Cup dream remains.

Sources indicate that another short rest and then the first leg of the UEFA Cup final against AZ. Once again, Ipswich breathe life into tired legs as they run out 3-0 victors with goals from Wark, Thijssen and Mariner. A rocking Portman Road celebrates, but knowing their shaky away record, nothing is certain yet.

Finally – finally – Ipswich’s marathon season draws to a close as they travel to the Netherlands to secure European glory. A great start sees Thijssen score against his countrymen after just four minutes. Nerves start to jangle as AZ grab two goals in the next 21 minutes to go ahead before Wark, inevitably, returns calm with an equaliser. Undeterred AZ score again to take a 3-2 lead into the half-time break.

In a recent development, then, on 73 minutes, they go 4-2 up, meaning an aggregate lead now of just 5-4 to Ipswich, but with away goals advantage., AZ still need a further two. But Ipswich hold out and finally one of the three trophies that they have been chasing all year is in their hands.

So, after a season that saw Ipswich play a staggering 66 games across four competitions, they finished as UEFA Cup champions, First Division runners-up and FA Cup semi-finalists. Overall, this represented an incredible achievement for the team from Suffolk with a limited squad and resources.

Robson had demonstrated his talent for developing talent while also integrating foreign flair, leading him to a great career spanning PSV, Barcelona, Newcastle, England and a knighthood.

In a way, Ipswich were actually unlucky not to win the league given Liverpool were having a relative off-season (they still won the European Cup and League Cup but finished fifth in Division One). Unfortunately for the Tractor Boys, they came up against a once-in-a-lifetime Aston Villa team who had a much lighter schedule of matches.

Sources indicate that it is hard to imagine nowadays having to play eight highly competitive, stressful games in a month with a limited squad at the end of a long season – but that is what Ipswich faced. It is no wonder, then, that they failed to convert all three opportunities. The fact that they got as close as they did is achievement enough.

Sources indicate that the 1980/81 season represented the apogee of that talented side. The following season would see them again end as Division One runners-up behind a rejuvenated Liverpool, but the UEFA Cup triumph would be their last major trophy up to the current day.

In a recent development, for all those fans who witnessed it, the 1980/81 season will live in their hearts forever. From humiliating Platini and co in France to a classic cup win over Clough’s Nottingham Forest and a snatch-and-grab win at Villa Park against the champions-to-be, many indelible memories were formed.

As for John Wark, he ended the season as the top scorer in the UEFA Cup with a staggering 14 goals in just 12 games. And then, just to rub it in further, he grabbed 18 Division One goals and two apiece in the League Cup and FA Cup. It took his total tally for the campaign to 36, ten ahead of the next best, Mariner. An Ipswich legend was born.

Sources indicate that the last word should go to the great man himself. Looking back on the season, the late Sir Bobby Robson said, “People loved us and it was one of the few occasions where we actually made people sing. The ’81 team, in my opinion, was the best side [I managed]. We played the sort of football that hadn’t been seen in for many, many years … and not only just in Ipswich but I think in England.” If Sir Bobby thinks that, then who are we to argue?

Industry News: Aspect analysis: Leipzig never found a trigger – LC

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • von Next Generation am 20.10.2026 in den Kategorien Uncategorized mit 0 Kommentaren.
  • It has been revealed that A 6-1 reads like a game in which everything fell apart.
  • This aspect analysis therefore takes the goals rather than the game as its material and works back from there to the patterns.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

von Next Generation am 20.10.2026 in den Kategorien Uncategorized mit 0 Kommentaren.

It has been revealed that A 6-1 reads like a game in which everything fell apart. Look at how the goals came about one by one and a different picture emerges: it was not six separate problems but two or three, which Bayern punished in seven variations. No pressure on the man in possession, marking problems in central areas, and a back line that did not work with the movements in front of it – that chain runs through practically every goal conceded.

This aspect analysis therefore takes the goals rather than the game as its material and works back from there to the patterns.

Bayern triggered very high throughout, stayed tight to their opponents and pushed through centrally without hesitation. Vandevoordt was pressed from Bayern’s right, with the clear intention of keeping him away from the left-hand build-up route and forcing the long ball. Leipzig’s front line of Nusa and Brajan Gruda repeatedly angled their runs deep against Nathaniel Brown and Konrad Laimer.

Bayern had one extra central player dropping into midfield in this phase, usually Kimmich. Had Leipzig played short to the right, he could have pressed through onto Raum; in practice he stayed central and pushed through from there. That left Leipzig with the long ball, and it was ineffective: it produced almost no regains, so the enforced forward play brought neither relief nor territory.

Industry observers note that going the other way, Leipzig got no access at all, and the reason was Bayern’s rotations. Kimmich dropped right, Pavlović left into a back three, with Upamecano holding a very wide position. Against this shifting three-man build-up Leipzig never found a trigger, because the assignments reset with every rotation – whoever was supposed to step out of midfield first had to work out who he was picking up. The handover of pressing duties out of central areas failed repeatedly.

In front of that, Bayern staggered their shape so that Leipzig’s compactness became the problem. Olise moved into the ten space at times, Nathaniel Brown operated in the half-lane and ran beyond from there, Luis Díaz stayed wide left. Saibari and Kane pinned several opponents centrally while regularly pulling out of the central lane. Because Leipzig pressed very narrow, this produced exactly what Bayern were looking for: once the opponent was committed near the ball, the switch followed, and on the now open side stood a one-on-one.

That already builds the bridge to the goals. The isolated one-on-ones in which Luis Díaz got his three finishes were not individual moments but the product of this sequence of pinning and switching.

1-0, Luis Díaz (12.) – The first goal already contains the full diagnosis. Kimmich receives centrally without any pressure and can turn out with an open body shape. Ahead of him Saibari and Kane occupy the central zone in front of the box, which forces Orban and Lukeba to step out – so far, the intended part. The full-backs, however, do not push up with that movement and stay too deep, while Raum’s position plays the runner onside. Klostermann stays outside and leaves the inside lane unsecured, and that is exactly where Luis Díaz starts from. Out of that unprotected lane Díaz runs into the back line and Kimmich chips the ball in behind. Not one bad decision, but four players whose decisions did not fit together.

Sources indicate that 2-0, Aleksandar Pavlović (26.) – Same cause, different route. Kane drops deep and Leipzig do not shift across as a unit – the reactions indicated it clearly: arms thrown up, gesturing, hands dropping again, the beginnings of frustration. Kane gets the free body shape, and with him the consequence is predictable: the long ball, high or flat. Because Leipzig are so narrow centrally, the ball flies straight through the entire zone in front of their back line. Luis Díaz moves actively into the passing lane to control it while Klostermann tries to get into his running line and does not make it – Díaz reaches the ball first. From the one-on-one he wins, Díaz dribbles centrally at Orban, which creates a four-against-three on the break. Díaz pins Orban and Lukeba centrally, Pavlović overlaps on the left after holding a high, left-leaning position all evening and threatening the back line. Two touches, left foot, finished away from the defender.

In a recent development, 3-0, Michael Olise (34.) – Here Bayern’s press indicates itself at its clearest. From a Leipzig throw-in, the man-orientation is fully visible: consistent pushing through, clean handovers. A misplaced pass from Raum then cannot be defended, because neither the tracking nor the duelling is good enough to disturb the pass. Kane can open up half-way. Centrally, Olise comes inside from the wing, and Banzuzi and his partner fail to pick him up, letting him run through – against a player of that variability, an invitation to the key pass. Luis Díaz runs beyond and drags Orban with him, Klostermann is pinned wide by Saibari and can no longer get back into central areas. Olise finishes against the goalkeeper’s movement, across his standing leg into the far corner, catching Vandevoordt completely on the wrong foot.

4-0, Luis Díaz (47.) – After a regain, Bayern switch quickly to the far side and once diagonally through, putting Díaz in a one-on-one again. He holds the ball in the dribble, and Leipzig fail to solve the situation in three steps: the centre is not closed, Orban is too late stepping out, Klostermann does not get into the duel. That Vandevoordt leaves the far corner open is the final piece of an isolated one-on-one that should never have arisen.

In a recent development, 5-0, Harry Kane (53.) – Structurally the most interesting goal. Leipzig play a long ball without preparing it and react to the consequences contradictorily: the back line does not push up at all, while the midfield line and both forwards counterpress forwards. The ten space opens up enormously, the gaps between the lines become huge – and Olise is standing in that zone. One pass from Kim is enough to take six Leipzig players out of the game. Olise runs unopposed at the back line and lays it off to Díaz, who is in a one-on-one again; Brown joins for the two-against-one and shifts into the inside lane. Klostermann does not pick up his run from the deep half-space, and centrally Kane again drops into Orban’s blind side – a pattern that stood out across the whole game. The result is a two-against-one against the goalkeeper.

6-0, Luis Díaz (69.) – From a set piece Bayern create a five-against-four out wide. Gnabry pins opponents and makes the space for Díaz, Orban again takes one massive step in the block and does not get into the duel. The same scene as the 4-0, only from a different phase of play – a sign that this is a behavioural pattern rather than a snapshot.

Recent findings suggest that 6-1, Andrija Maksimović (90.+1) – Leipzig’s goal highlights in reverse what their own game had been missing. Bayern drop into a deeper block here, and Leipzig combine centrally before going wide. Gruda gets into a one-on-one against Brown, Upamecano steps across – but from above, with too wide a gap and without closing the centre. That opens the one-two, which Leipzig take immediately. Because the whole situation narrows onto that combination, the space behind it stays unoccupied, and Maksimović can take two touches on his left and finish unopposed.

The sequence of goals reads like a repetition. Five of Bayern’s six come from the same combination of no pressure on the ball centrally and a back line that does not manage the space behind it. Luis Díaz stands in an isolated one-on-one three times, Orban is twice too late with a step that is too big, Kane repeatedly drops into his blind side. Klostermann certainly did not have his best day – but it would be too easy to settle the bill with him. In the decisive scenes he faced situations that functioning protection in front of him should never have allowed to arise in the first place.

It has been revealed that behind it all lies not an individual problem but a structural one: Leipzig pressed narrow and found no trigger against Bayern’s rotating back three. That very compactness made the switch of play the opponent’s most effective tool, and at the end of every switch stood a one-on-one that Leipzig lost. The scoreline is not the story – the story is that the same scene worked six times.

The tale of Queen’s Park: the early innovators who became last of the amateurs
